# agentterm

> Run long-lived processes the agent can read, write to and wait on.
> Stop wrapping dev servers in `&`.

**agentterm** is a PTY layer for coding agents: an OpenCode plugin, an MCP server for
harnesses that are not OpenCode, and a standalone web terminal — like tmux, but
agent-native.

[![CI](https://github.com/lenucksi/opencode-pty/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/lenucksi/opencode-pty/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Coverage](https://img.shields.io/badge/coverage-80%25+-brightgreen)](https://github.com/lenucksi/opencode-pty)
[![Version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@lenucksi%2Fagentterm)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lenucksi/agentterm)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)

A plugin for [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) that gives the agent real PTY sessions:
run dev servers, watchers, REPLs and TUIs in the background, send them input, read
their output on demand, and get notified when they exit. Multiple sessions, real
terminal emulation, a web UI and a TUI panel.

**Status:** actively maintained on `local/modernized` (1.0.1), published as
`@lenucksi/agentterm`. Fork of
[shekohex/opencode-pty](https://github.com/shekohex/opencode-pty); features are kept in a
shape that can be contributed upstream. The plugin id, the daemon socket and the state
directory keep the name `opencode-pty`: renaming them would orphan the archive and the
sidebar preferences of every existing install.

![agentterm in the browser](docs/media/web-ui-demo.gif)

![agentterm's TUI panel in OpenCode](docs/media/tui-demo.gif)

## Why agentterm?

tmux is built for a human attached to a terminal. agentterm is built for a model that
reads and types, and for a human who wants to watch the same process: a **PTY** layer,
not a pipe.

|                                | tmux                    | agentterm                                                                      |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Who reads it                   | a human, attached       | the agent: byte-exact paging with an offset cursor, regex filter, token budget |
| Who watches                    | a human                 | the human, in the browser, on the same process                                 |
| Waiting for new output         | polling in the terminal | `pty_wait`, or a `<pty_exited>` message, instead of polling                    |
| Programs that need a TTY       | yes                     | yes — a real PTY: mouse reporting, true colour, alternate screen               |
| What outlives the session      | the tmux server         | the daemon                                                                     |
| How the agent knows it is over | —                       | `<pty_exited>` (OpenCode) / `pty_wait` (MCP)                                   |

The word **PTY** is in the name of every tool for that reason: it is what people and
models type when they are looking for this.

OpenCode v2 can background shell calls — so this plugin isn't about _whether_ a process
runs in the background. It's about **real terminal emulation** and **shared control**:

- **Processes that need a TTY** — certain Ansible plays, SSH sessions, anything that prompts or formats for a terminal.
- **Long-running serial connections** — a VM's EFI/boot manager, a serial console you drive for minutes or hours.
- **Interactive programs** — REPLs, `top`, `vim`, prompts, TUIs.
- **Dev servers & watchers** (`bun run dev`, `cargo watch`, `bun test --watch`).

With a PTY, the agent and a human can send input to the _same_ running process, short or
long-lived, and both watch it through the web UI or the TUI panel. You get a real terminal
buffer with byte-exact paging, mouse reporting, selection, true colour, and exit
notifications instead of polling — like tmux, but agent-native.

## Install

OpenCode V2 (recommended):

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugin": [{ "package": "@lenucksi/agentterm", "options": { "port": 4200, "autostart": true } }]
}
```

`@lenucksi/agentterm` and `@lenucksi/agentterm/v2` are the same plugin — the bare name loads the V2
half, so a configuration that names either works. The TUI half is `@lenucksi/agentterm/v2/tui`,
and the host finds it by itself when the plugin directory has one.

This plugin needs OpenCode 2.x: the V1 plugin shape is gone, and the V2 half is the
only one there is.

### Not OpenCode? MCP.

The same eight tools, over MCP, for a harness that speaks it — Claude Code, Codex:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pty": { "command": "bunx", "args": ["-p", "@lenucksi/agentterm", "agentterm-mcp"] }
  }
}
```

Same daemon, same sessions, same result tags — a session an MCP client starts is a
session the OpenCode plugin lists. The texts, the permission gate and the completion
signal are the route's own: see [`docs/mcp.md`](docs/mcp.md). The web interface is
also a binary of its own (`bunx -p @lenucksi/agentterm agentterm-web`) for a human who wants to watch.

## Where to find it

- **As an OpenCode plugin** — `@lenucksi/agentterm` in `opencode.json`; the TUI panel is
  found by the host from the package itself. The plugin id it reports is `opencode-pty`.
- **As an MCP server** — the same package ships `agentterm-mcp`, an MCP stdio server for
  harnesses that are not OpenCode (Claude Code, Codex, anything that speaks MCP). It is
  not a Bash replacement: the eight `pty_*` tools are added next to whatever shell tool
  the harness already has.
- **As a web terminal** — `agentterm-web` serves the same interface against the daemon,
  loopback by default.
- **Search terms that find it** — `pty`, `terminal`, `tmux`, `mcp`, `mcp-server`,
  `opencode-plugin`. The repository carries those as GitHub topics, the package as npm
  keywords, and the description names PTY, terminal, MCP and OpenCode in one sentence.

## Try it

Ask the agent: _"Start `bun run dev` as a background session and tell me when it's ready."_
It will call `pty_spawn`, wait for `<pty_exited>`/`pty_wait`, and report the URL.

## One session, end to end

```
pty_spawn: command="bun", args=["run","dev"], description="Dev server", title="Dev Server"
→ <pty_spawned id="pty_a1b2c3d4" cols="240" rows="80">

pty_read:  id="pty_a1b2c3d4", limit=50
→ last 50 lines of output

pty_read:  id="pty_a1b2c3d4", pattern="error|ERROR", ignoreCase=true
→ only the matching lines

pty_write: id="pty_a1b2c3d4", data="\x03"
→ Ctrl+C

pty_kill:  id="pty_a1b2c3d4", cleanup=true
→ terminated and freed
```

## Why this over the alternatives

- **vs. OpenCode's `bash` tool**: `bash` blocks until the process exits. PTYs run in the background and the agent reads, writes and waits on its own schedule — and gives the agent a real terminal, not a pipe.
- **vs. `tmux`/`screen`**: no second tool to learn, no pane to attach to. Sessions are first-class objects the agent can list, resize, screenshot and kill, with a web UI and a TUI panel.
- **vs. shelling out with `&`**: real terminal emulation (mouse reporting, selection, true colour), a bounded output buffer with byte-exact paging, and exit notifications instead of polling.

## Common invocations

```bash
# Dev server, sized for a wide terminal
pty_spawn({ command: "bun", args: ["run","dev"], description: "Dev server", cols: 200, rows: 50 })

# Serial console (raw line discipline — Enter arrives as CR, not LF)
pty_spawn({ command: "virsh", args: ["-c","qemu:///system","console","--force","myguest"],
            description: "Guest serial console", raw: true })

# Build, then wait for it
pty_spawn({ command: "npm", args: ["run","build"], description: "Build", notifyOnExit: true })
pty_wait({ id: "pty_..." })

# Full-screen program as a screen, not a byte stream
pty_screen({ id: "pty_..." })
```

## Configuration

Environment variables (full table in [`docs/configuration.md`](docs/configuration.md)):

| Variable               | Default      | What it does              |
| ---------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------- |
| `PTY_MAX_BUFFER_LINES` | `50000`      | Lines kept per session    |
| `PTY_READ_MAX_TOKENS`  | `25000`      | Default `pty_read` budget |
| `PTY_WEB_PORT`         | `0` (random) | Web UI port               |
| `PTY_WEB_HOSTNAME`     | `::1`        | Web UI bind host          |

Plugin options (V2): `port`, `hostname`, `autostart`, `retention`. Archive retention
(`maxSessions`, `maxAgeDays`, `maxBytesPerSession`) is enforced on the shared on-disk
archive; see `docs/configuration.md`.

Permissions: the model's `pty_spawn`/`pty_write` calls go through OpenCode's own
permission system — the same rules and the same prompt the built-in `bash` tool uses.
The web interface has no session to ask about, so it starts what you asked for.
See `docs/configuration.md`.

## Status, versioning, upgrade

- **Status**: actively maintained on `local/modernized` (1.0.0). Fork of
  [shekohex/opencode-pty](https://github.com/shekohex/opencode-pty); features are kept in a
  shape that can be contributed upstream.
- **Versioning**: SemVer. Breaking changes get a major bump.
- **Upgrade**: OpenCode checks for plugin updates on startup. Force a clean reinstall with
  `rm -rf ~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/opencode-pty && opencode`.

## Web UI & TUI panel

- **Web UI**: React/xterm, real-time WebSocket streaming, mouse selection, themes,
  download, session groups, coloured output. Start with `/pty-open-background-spy`.
- **TUI panel**: a PTY section in OpenCode's sidebar (2.0.23+) and a per-conversation
  session panel (`/pty-sessions`), with coloured output, scrollback and a command line.
- **REST API + WebSocket**: see [`docs/api.md`](docs/api.md).
- **Version identity**: `GET /api/server` and the Settings dialog show the build's
  version and the commit it was built from.

## How it works

1. **Spawn**: bun-pty runs the command in the background.
2. **Buffer**: rolling ring buffer (default 1 MB) with absolute character offsets.
3. **Read**: byte-exact paging via `since`; regex filtering; whole-result token budget.
4. **Screen**: `pty_screen` replays the buffer through the same VT parser the web UI uses.
5. **Write**: any input, including escape sequences.
6. **Lifecycle**: sessions persist until cleanup; auto-cleanup on session end.
7. **Notify**: `notifyOnExit` sends a `<pty_exited>` message.

More detail: [`docs/how-it-works.md`](docs/how-it-works.md), [`docs/diagrams.md`](docs/diagrams.md).

# Patches

Dependency patches applied by `bun install` (see `patchedDependencies` in
`package.json`).

## `ghostty-web.patch`

**Upstream:** `anomalyco/ghostty-web` (pinned to `6e24d04`).
**Remove when:** the fix is released upstream and the pin points to a commit that contains it.

`Terminal.reset()` frees the WASM terminal it was built with and creates a
replacement. Components created during `open()` could retain the freed instance,
so they kept reading stale state after a reset:

- `SelectionManager.getSelection()` returned empty cells, so copying a
  highlighted block produced blank lines only;
- selection dimensions came from the old instance (for example 80x24), which
  clamped selection and highlighting to the stale grid;
- application mouse-mode callbacks could continue querying the freed terminal
  instead of the replacement buffer.

The patch resolves selection and mouse-mode state from the terminal's current
WASM instance, clears selection state before freeing the old instance, and keeps
the existing Shift override for native text selection. The application triggers
`reset()` whenever the raw stream is re-seeded (session switch, buffer snapshot,
gap resync), which is why the bug was easy to hit in normal use.

### Backport: resolved black backgrounds

`anomalyco/ghostty-web#8` (`4a7026e`) fixes explicit RGB black cell
backgrounds on non-black themes. The renderer used to treat every resolved
`(0, 0, 0)` cell as transparent, even though Ghostty had already resolved the
application's requested color. The patch paints that cell as real black while
preserving selection and inverse-video precedence.

Remove this hunk when the pin points to a commit containing the upstream fix.

### Backport: fragmented OSC color queries

`anomalyco/ghostty-web#9` (`5006e8e`) replaces the regex-based OSC 10/11
observer with bounded byte-wise parser state. The backport handles fragmented
string and binary writes, combined foreground/background queries, matching BEL
or ST reply terminators, cancellation, escape interruption, and terminal reset.
It also refreshes Ghostty's render state before returning resolved colors.

The scope remains 7-bit OSC foreground/background queries. Raw C1 controls,
additional color slots, and per-query snapshots interleaved with color changes
inside one WASM write remain outside this patch.

Remove this hunk when the pin points to a commit containing the upstream fix.

Terminates a running PTY session.

Use this tool to:
- Stop a running process (sends SIGTERM)

Usage:
- `id`: The PTY session ID (from pty_spawn or pty_list)
- `cleanup`: Deprecated — remove finished sessions from the human web UI instead.

Behavior:
- If the session is running, it will be killed (status becomes "killed")
- If cleanup=false (default), the session remains in the list with its output buffer intact
- If cleanup=true, the session is removed entirely and the buffer is freed

Deprecation:
- Never pass `cleanup: true`. It frees the session's entire output buffer, and
  that buffer is the only record of what the process did.
- This includes sessions you created for your own verification. "The human may
  still want to inspect it" is not a reason to keep one and "this session is
  mine, so it does not count" is not a reason to delete one: a model that frees
  a buffer to save tokens destroys the evidence it would need to explain a
  failure, and measured across 15 real runs, 4 did exactly that - including
  deleting the very output they were in the middle of reading, and noting it as
  "expected".
- Kill the session and leave it in the list. Removing it is a human's decision,
  made in the web UI.

Tips:
- To send Ctrl+C instead of killing, use pty_write with data="\x03"

Lists all PTY sessions (active and exited) with their status, PID, line count,
character count and current terminal size.

A session with a large character count but almost no lines is painting a screen;
`pty_screen` returns what that screen looks like.

Reads output from a running or completed PTY session.

Use it to look at what a session printed - the buffer survives process exit, so
reading a finished session is normal, not an error.

Usage:
- `id`: The PTY session ID (from `pty_spawn` or `pty_list`)
- `offset`: 0-based line to start from (default: 0)
- `limit`: how many lines to return (default: 500)
- `pattern`: regex; only matching lines are returned, then `offset`/`limit` apply to the matches
- `ignoreCase`: make `pattern` case-insensitive (default: false)
- `maxTokens`: raise the result budget in tokens (capped by the server ceiling)
- `since`: absolute character offset to resume from; returns the raw stream from
  that point with no line numbering
- `all`: remove the result budget entirely. Unbounded - can overflow your context.

Behavior:
- A result is capped at 25000 tokens (about 100000 characters) unless you pass
  `maxTokens`; the server caps the request at 125000 tokens. The cap applies to
  the whole result, not per line.
- When the cap bites, the `<pty_output>` tag carries `truncated="true"`,
  `chars="shown/total"` and `nextSince="N"`, and the cut line ends in a
  `… [truncated: X of Y chars]` marker. That is not the end of the data.
- To continue without losing or repeating a character, read with
  `pty_read({ id, since: N })` and follow each `nextSince` until the tag omits it.
  `offset`/`limit` are line-based and cannot resume inside a cut line.
- `since` and `offset` are mutually exclusive; `since` wins.
- A `pattern` that looks like catastrophic backtracking (nested repeated groups,
  stacked non-greedy quantifiers, long alternations) is rejected with an error.
  Simplify it, or fetch the window first and filter yourself.

A large character count with almost no lines means the program is repainting a
screen rather than printing lines. `pty_screen` returns that screen; this output
cannot express its layout.

To wait for a process to finish instead of polling, use `pty_wait`. {{skill}}

Sets the terminal size of a running PTY session.

The process is told immediately (SIGWINCH), so full-screen programs redraw at the
new geometry. Programs that only read the size once, at startup, need a `pty_spawn`
with `cols`/`rows` instead.

Usage:
- `id`: The PTY session ID
- `cols`: Terminal width in columns. Omit to keep the current width.
- `rows`: Terminal height in rows. Omit to keep the current height.

Behavior:
- Both dimensions are clamped to sane bounds; an omitted dimension is left alone
  rather than reset, so resizing only the width does not silently change the
  height.
- The new size is reported back and is also visible in `pty_list`.
- Only the size changes. It does not clear the buffer, and it works on an exited
  session's record but has no effect on a process that is already gone.

To start a session at a specific size instead, pass `cols`/`rows` to `pty_spawn`.

Replays a PTY session's output through a terminal emulator and returns the screen.

Use this instead of `pty_read` when you need to know what a program *looks like* -
a TUI, a pager, `top`, `htop`, a progress display, anything that paints a screen.
For ordinary line-oriented output such as a build log, `pty_read` is cheaper and
its line numbers line up with what the process printed.

Usage:
- `id`: The PTY session ID
- `colors`: include the colour and style of every run of cells that differ from
  the default (default: false). Off by default because it costs tokens and most
  questions are about layout, not colour.
- `width`: render at this many columns instead of the session's own width. Use it
  to see how a program behaves at a size you care about; the session's real
  geometry is left untouched.
- `height`: same, for rows

Behavior:
- The screen is rebuilt by replaying the retained output, so it is what a user
  looking at the session would see, not the last thing the process wrote.
- Trailing blank columns are dropped from each row. A row is still exactly
  `height` rows tall; blank rows come back empty.
- A wide character (CJK, emoji) occupies one grid cell but is two columns wide,
  so a row's text can be wider on screen than its cell count suggests.
- If the session's retained output is larger than one replay window, the tail is
  used and the response says so. A row the program painted long ago and never
  touched again will not be in that window.

Output:
- `<pty_screen>` carries `cols`, `rows`, the cursor as `cursor="x,y"`, whether
  the cursor is visible, and whether the program is on the alternate screen.
- The body is the screen, one row per line, each prefixed with its row number.
- With `colors: true`, a `<pty_spans>` block follows, listing runs as
  `row col length style`, e.g. `3 4 9 fg=#5fd75f bold`.
- `scrollback` is the number of lines above the screen. Read those with
  `pty_read`; they are not part of the screen.

Cost: the replay is proportional to the retained output and bounded by the
buffer cap. It is a read of the program's *state*, not a poll: prefer one call
over repeated ones.

Sends named keys to a running PTY session.

Use this instead of `pty_write` when what you want to press has a name: it saves you
from knowing that Enter is `\r`, that ArrowUp is `\x1b[A`, or that Ctrl-C is a single
byte. The result says which key was sent, so a key that did nothing is visible in the
transcript rather than in a prompt that never moved.

Usage:
- `id`: The PTY session ID
- `key`: The key by name (case-insensitive)
- `times`: How often to send it (default 1, at most 100)

Keys:
- `Enter`, `Tab`, `Escape` (or `Esc`), `Space`, `Backspace`, `Delete`, `Insert`
- `Up`, `Down`, `Left`, `Right`, `Home`, `End`, `PageUp` (or `PgUp`), `PageDown`
- `C-a` through `C-z` (also written `Ctrl-a`), and `C-space`
- `F1` through `F12`

Behavior:
- Only named keys go through this tool. **A command is still typed with `pty_write`**,
  where the permission policy sees the line - this tool cannot enter text, so it
  cannot be used to route around that check.
- A name the terminal does not have is refused with the list of names that exist; it
  is not silently sent as text.
- Sending keys to an exited session fails; the record stays readable with `pty_read`.

Example:
- `pty_write` `"ls -la"`, then `pty_sendkey` `Enter` - rather than `pty_write` `"ls -la\r"`.
- `pty_sendkey` `Down` with `times: 3` to move three rows in a menu.
- `pty_sendkey` `C-c` to interrupt a program that is printing.

Creates a PTY session for any command that should run in the background, needs interactive input, persists beyond the current response, or is long-running.

Use it instead of the built-in bash tool for dev servers, watch modes, local APIs, REPLs and TUIs - anything you may need to send input to, or read while it runs.

Usage:
- `command` (required), `args`, `workdir`, `env`, `title`
- `description` (required): a clear, concise 5-10 word description
- `notifyOnExit`: {{notifyOnExit}}
- `timeoutSeconds`: hard cap. Skip it for processes meant to keep running unless the user asks; set it for builds, tests, e2e runs or migrations you are waiting on
- `cols`, `rows`: terminal geometry. Defaults to the size the web UI last reported, or 240x80 when no client is attached. Set it when the program formats for a width, prints wide lines or draws a full-screen UI
- `raw`: run with the PTY line discipline disabled (`stty raw -echo`). Set it for a serial console (`virsh console`) or any program that wants a `\r` to stay a `\r` - otherwise the kernel turns Enter into `\n` and the program ignores it. Do NOT use it for a shell: it turns off echo, line editing and the interrupt key. When it is set, write only after the program has produced output, because the discipline is switched by a wrapper just before your command starts.

The result tag is `<pty_spawned id="..." cols="C" rows="R">`. Read the id from
that tag - not from the `ID:` line below it, which repeats the same value for
readability. The id is the input to every other tool in this family, so this is
the one result worth reading mechanically. The tag also carries the geometry the
session got; the body repeats it as `Size: <cols>x<rows>`.

Output folded onto the wrong line is a geometry problem until proven otherwise.
`pty_resize` changes the size of a running session, but a program that read its
size at startup will not react to that - respawn with `cols`/`rows` instead.

Then use `pty_write` (input), `pty_read` (output), `pty_wait` (block until it exits), `pty_list`, `pty_resize`, `pty_kill`.
{{completion}}

{{skill}}

Waits for a PTY session to finish, or — with `quietMs` — for it to go quiet.

Use it after `pty_spawn` when you need the exit status, and after `pty_write` when you
need to know the program has finished reacting before you read again. It returns when
the session ends, so you do not poll `pty_read` in a loop.

Usage:
- `id`: The PTY session ID
- `timeoutSeconds`: Maximum time to wait. If the session is still running after
  this, returns a `<pty_wait_timeout>` result instead of blocking forever.
  Default: no limit on the OpenCode route, the route's cap on MCP.
- `quietMs`: Return once the session has printed nothing for this many
  milliseconds. **The session keeps running** — this is how you wait for a shell
  prompt after sending a command, without a loop.

Behavior:
- With `quietMs`, the wait ends on whichever comes first: the session printing
  nothing for that long, the session exiting, or the timeout. The result says which,
  in its `reason` attribute (`quiet` or `exit`).
- A quiet result is not a completion: the process is still running and `Exit:` is
  absent, because there is no exit status yet.
- The output position is sampled a few times a second, never finer than the window
  you asked for. A very small `quietMs` therefore measures your sample, not the
  program — 200-500 ms is the range a prompt actually needs.
- On a session that has already ended, both forms return at once with
  `reason="exit"`.
- The heartbeat keeps a long wait alive on a transport that would cut a silent call;
  with `quietMs` the same applies.

Examples:
- `pty_write` `"make test"`, then `pty_wait` `{ quietMs: 500 }` — the prompt is back.
- `pty_spawn` a build, then `pty_wait` `{ timeoutSeconds: 600 }` — the exit status.
Sends input (text or escape sequences) to a running PTY session.
